forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Reorganized parishes budget £202,000 for neighbourhood wardens and triple youth work spending
news_drafts.lead:
The reorganized parish council formed from three separate authorities is planning significant service expansions as it sets its budget for 2027/28. Neighbourhood warden costs more than double to £202,498, including provision for two additional staff members. Youth work spending increases tenfold to £60,000 from £6,000. The new unified authority, which will employ 11 staff including clerks and administrators at a cost of £559,000, is anticipated to hold £210,000 in reserves sourced from North Horsham Parish Council. However, residents face sharply divergent impacts on their precepts: Roffey Parish residents face a 36 per cent reduction of £26.89 on a Band D property, while Horsham Town Council residents see a 15 per cent decrease and North Horsham residents a 3 per cent rise. The budget provisions £10,000 for system harmonization between the previously separate parishes.

---

news_drafts.headline: Horsham faces £1m budget shortfall by 2028 as government support grant ends
news_drafts.lead: Horsham Council projected a £1 million budget deficit by 2028/29 when a one-year government support grant expires, its Audit Committee heard on 16 September. The deficit reflects a combination of reduced central government funding and only 0.1 per cent assumed growth in the council's income. The council has already flagged a likely deficit in 2027/28 following the final government spending settlement, which reduced its core spending power by 4.3 per cent. The council balanced its 2026/27 budget only through use of the temporary support grant. Officials noted that a local government reorganisation scheduled by 2029 may mean Horsham will not need to deliver the savings required, but the structural funding gap is real and will require a financial plan if the council remains as currently configured.

findings.headline: Reorganized authority anticipated to hold £210,000 reserves at 31 March 2027, sourced from NHPC reserves
findings.detail: The budget projects opening reserves of £210,000 at the end of the first financial year of the reorganized authority, drawn from North Horsham Parish Council reserves. This represents the balance sheet position post-merger and forms the financial cushion for the new combined entity.
findings.matters: Reserve position indicates financial resilience and buffer for unforeseen costs or revenue shortfalls; material for assessing creditworthiness and financial sustainability post-reorganization

findings.headline: Administrative and professional services costs doubled across the board for 'increased electorate' without quantifying growth
findings.detail: Multiple administrative line items double from 2026/27 to 2027/28 with the notation 'Doubled to account for increased electorate, and 5% increase'. These include insurance (£16,500→£34,650), subscriptions (£3,800→£7,980), external audit (£1,500→£3,150), professional services (£4,250→£8,925), and others. The paper does not quantify electorate growth or provide baseline comparisons.
findings.matters: Doubling of administrative costs requires understanding whether driven by genuine electorate growth or administrative expansion; lenders assess budget robustness and inflation assumptions
findings.figures: Insurance £16,500→£34,650, Subscriptions £3,800→£7,980, External Audit £1,500→£3,150, Professional Services £4,250→£8,925
findings.quote: Doubled to account for increased electorate, and 5% increase

findings.headline: Neighbourhood warden service expanded by 2 additional FTE, budget doubling from £98,300 to £202,498
findings.detail: Neighbourhood warden costs more than double from £98,300 to £202,498, with the budget paper explicitly stating 'provision for 2 additional wardens' beyond current staffing. This represents a significant service expansion and staffing commitment, though the paper does not explain the demand or policy driver.
findings.matters: Service expansion signals policy commitment or demand increase; lenders assess whether recurring spending commitments are justified and sustainable
findings.quote: Neighbourhood wardens 98,300.00£ 202,498.00£ 3% increase staff costs, plus provision for 2 additional wardens

findings.headline: Roffey Parish Council precept declining 36.31% post-reorganization with no explanation provided
findings.detail: Different areas of the reorganized authority face sharply divergent precept impacts. RPC residents face a Band D reduction of £26.89 (36.31% decline) with no explanation in the paper. HTC residents face a 15.54% reduction (£8.68 Band D) attributed to withdrawal of the special charge under review. NHPC residents see a modest 3.13% increase (£1.43 Band D). The unexplained RPC decline raises questions about service provision or financial arrangements.
findings.matters: Uneven precept impacts across merged areas signal resource redistribution and potential merger tensions; unexplained 36% reduction warrants scrutiny of whether services are being reduced or funded differently

findings.headline: Youth work budget increases 900% from £6,000 to £60,000 with only 'increased provision' cited
findings.detail: Youth work expenditure is budgeted to increase tenfold from £6,000 in 2026/27 to £60,000 in 2027/28. The only explanation provided in the budget paper is the notation 'Increased provision', with no detail on demand drivers, service specification, outcomes, or justification for this commitment.
findings.matters: Unexplained service commitments of this magnitude signal uncertain budget planning; lenders assess whether recurring spending is sustainable and grounded in genuine demand
